newsitem.title: BELGIUM: US move to limit NATO enlargement due to cost concerns.
newsitem.headline: US move to limit NATO enlargement due to cost concerns.

text.p: The United States decision to announce publicly it wants to limit NATO enlargement to three countries later this summer has been prompted by growing opposition in the Republican-led Congress to the costs of enlargement, NATO analysts say.

Washington said on Thursday it wanted Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic to join the alliance, stunning some of its European allies and dismaying the two other main hopefuls -- Romania and Slovenia which immediately vowed to battle on.

Some European ministers, angered by what they see as a clear attempt to cut short debate on the issue ahead of a summit in Madrid on July 8-9, openly criticised the decision and pledged to try and have it overturned.
Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said it was a mistake. "I don't agree with this solution," he told reporters.
But NATO officials and diplomats say opposition to NATO enlargement, led by political heavyweights such as Henry Kissinger, has steadily grown in the U.S. over the last year.
Such critics argue it will effectively destroy the organisation, which won the Cold War without a shot being fired, and cost billions of dollars at a time of no obvious security threat.
"The U.S. knows it will have a battle to get three (new members) through Congress, let alone any more," said one diplomatic source.
Estimates of cost vary enormously with the military stressing it depends on how quickly and to what level the new countries' armed forces are modernised.

The U.S. administration calculates expansion could cost between $27-35 billion up to 2009, but says Washington would only have to pay $1.5-two billion. Other estimates are more than double those figures.

Each NATO member pays a proportion of its defence budget into a separate NATO budget used to pay for assets used or operated jointly by the alliance such as command and control centres. The more members there are the greater the joint expenditure.
Some members of Congress are also hostile to giving out more U.S. commitments to defend Europeans, pointing out the end of Cold War was expected to bring a reduction in such offers.

But President Bill Clinton increasingly sees alliance enlargement to include at least some of the West's former Warsaw Pact enemies as the major foreign policy objective of his second term and wants to avoid a serious row with Congress over costs.
"If Clinton had to choose between upsetting the allies or the Congress, he would choose the former," added the source.

The parliaments of all 16 current members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) have to ratify expansion after the new members are invited to join in Madrid, but only Congress is believed to pose a possible serious threat.
The allies have said they expect the ratification process to take two years so the new members could formally join the alliance in April 1999 -- the 50th anniversary of NATO's founding.

Supporters argue that would right the wrongs of history when the Yalta deal at the end of World War Two split Europe into communist East and non-communist West and anchor the new democracies firmly into the Western family of nations.
NATO operates by consensus, but the United States is by far its most important member and sources say it is inconceivable it could be overruled on the issue.
"The fact is everyone supports three, not everyone supports more than three, so three it is," said one NATO official.
But the U.S. move could further sour relations with France, which has strongly backed Romania and Slovenia.

Paris, which has failed to resolve a dispute with the U.S. over giving Europeans a greater role in the enlarged NATO, has been supported by Italy and other southern states arguing a broader enlargement is necessary to maintain a balance between the alliance's northern and southern flanks.

Senior U.S. officials counter that NATO enlargement was originally intended to complement European Union enlargement and say the European allies should advance that process as opposed to pushing for a broad alliance enlargement.
